research_issues.question: What limitation period applies under Georgia law to property damage claims, including damage to real property and personal property, and what rules may affect when the period begins or applies?

propositions.claim: For trespass upon or damage to real property, O.C.G.A. § 9-3-30 provides a four-year period after the right of action accrues.

For injuries to personal property, the 2024 Georgia Code text of O.C.G.A. § 9-3-31 provides four years after accrual; the 2025 text of § 9-3-32 likewise provides four years for recovery of personal property or damages for its conversion or destruction. The § 9-3-31 source is the 2024 edition.

For ordinary real-property damage, Georgia generally does not delay accrual until the damage is discovered. For a continuing nuisance treated as temporary, each continuation causing additional harm may give rise to a fresh action, with the limitations period running from that continuation.

sources.text: Mr. Justice Black delivered the opinion of the Court. Petitioner was charged in a Florida state court with having broken and entered a poolroom with intent to commit a misdemeanor. This offense is a felony under *337Florida law. Appearing in court without funds and without a lawyer, petitioner asked the court to appoint counsel for him, whereupon the following colloquy took place: “The Court: Mr. Gideon, I am sorry, but I cannot appoint Counsel to represent you in this case. Under the laws of the State of Florida, the only time the Court can appoint Counsel to represent a Defendant is when that person is charged with a capital offense. I am sorry, but I will have to deny your request to appoint Counsel to defend you in this case. “The Dependant: The United States Supreme Court says I am entitled to be represented by Counsel.” Put to trial before a jury, Gideon conducted his defense about as well as could be expected from a layman. He made an opening statement to the jury, cross-examined the State’s witnesses, presented witnesses in his own defense, declined to testify himself, and made a short argument “emphasizing his innocence to the charge contained in the Information filed in this case.” The jury returned a verdict of guilty, and petitioner was sentenced to serve five years in the state prison. Later, petitioner filed in the Florida Supreme Court this habeas corpus petition attacking his conviction and sentence on the ground that the trial court’s refusal to appoint counsel for him denied him rights “guaranteed by the Constitution and the Bill of Rights by the United States Government.” 1 Treating the petition for habeas corpus as properly before it, the State Supreme Court, “upon consideration thereof” but without an opinion, denied all relief. Unable to afford a lawyer, he asked the trial court to appoint counsel; the court denied the request because Florida appointed counsel only in capital cases. Gideon represented himself, was convicted by a jury, and sentenced to five years in prison. He then sought habeas relief in the Florida Supreme Court, which denied his petition without an opinion.

propositions.claim: The Court held that an indigent defendant in a criminal trial has a fundamental right to the assistance of counsel, essential to a fair trial, and that Gideon’s uncounseled trial and conviction violated the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court concluded that Betts v. Brady could not stand: the facts and circumstances of Betts and Gideon were nearly indistinguishable, yet applying Betts would require rejection of Gideon’s claim to constitutionally guaranteed counsel. On reconsideration, the Court overruled Betts.
